headline: Record-Breaking Rescue: 30 Beluga Whales Relocated to Safety
meta_description: SeaWorld and partner organizations completed the largest captive cetacean transport in U.S. history, relocating 30 beluga whales from a closed Canadian marine…
summary_short: SeaWorld San Antonio has completed the largest beluga whale rescue operation in U.S. history, welcoming 7 female whales as part of an unprecedented 2,000-mile relocation…
body:
A historic animal rescue unfolded across North America this summer when SeaWorld San Antonio and partner organizations successfully relocated 30 beluga whales from a shuttered marine park in Ontario, Canada, in what marks the largest captive cetacean transport ever undertaken by American zoos and aquariums. The second wave of the operation brought 7 female belugas—named Xena, Gemini, Skyla, Meeka, Eve, Neva, and Calypso—to San Antonio after a nearly 2,000-mile journey, where they now receive specialized veterinary care as they adjust to their new home. This unprecedented effort, coordinated by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums, underscores both the complexity and necessity of large-scale animal rescue in the modern world.

The logistics of moving such sensitive animals required extraordinary precision. Each group traveled in specialized water containers aboard aircraft with 24-hour veterinary supervision. Earlier in the operation, four female belugas had flown to Chicago's Shedd Aquarium via a Qatar Airways Boeing 777 container aircraft, arriving on July 22nd. The two male belugas, Frankie and Bertie Botts, arrived at SeaWorld three weeks prior and are already acclimating well to their new environment.

Currently, the seven female whales are housed in a private habitat away from public view while caretakers monitor each individual's adjustment at her own pace. Staff watch carefully for signs of healthy eating, comfortable rest, and early social interactions. SeaWorld's four decades of beluga care expertise proved essential to orchestrating this rescue. The organization's broader marine animal rescue program has assisted more than 43,000 animals throughout its history, making it one of the largest rescue operations of its kind in the United States. For these 30 belugas, the relocation represents a second chance at life beyond the confines of a facility that could no longer meet their needs.
